title: The clay lamp
hook: a thief took his iron lamp, so he bought a clay one, and the thief lost more (Discourses 1.18)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was blind: the wrongdoer has misjudged what's good. Your line was pity them instead.

Someone takes the package off your porch. Or your bike, or your lunch from the office fridge. It's small, but it stings for days. You replay it, check the doorbell camera, tell five people. Epictetus had something stolen too, and his reaction is one of the most famous little stories in the Discourses: a noise at the window, an empty spot by the shrine, and a cheaper replacement.
screen: `THE PACKAGE OFF YOUR PORCH.` → `IT STINGS FOR DAYS.` → `A NOISE AT THE WINDOW.`

segments.voice: It's still Discourses book one, chapter eighteen, right after the teaching about blindness. I kept an iron lamp, Epictetus tells his students, beside the little shrine of my household gods. I heard a noise at the window, ran down, and found it gone. Then I thought it over. The thief wanted a lamp; that's understandable. So tomorrow, I told myself, you'll find a clay one. A person only loses what they have. Notice the arithmetic. An iron lamp was a decent possession; a clay lamp costs very little and gives the same light. Epictetus lost almost nothing that mattered. The thief, as Epictetus sees it elsewhere in the Discourses, paid far more: for a lamp, he became a thief. He gave up his own honesty, which no one could have taken from him, for a piece of iron. Who lost more? Epictetus also explains why thieves make us so angry: we admire the things they take. If you didn't prize your clothes so much, he says, you wouldn't rage at the one who steals them. And there's a funny ending from outside the Discourses. The writer Lucian, a generation later, mocks a man who paid three thousand drachmas for Epictetus' clay lamp after the philosopher died, as if owning it would make him wise. The cheap lamp became an expensive treasure, exactly the kind of admiring Epictetus warned about.
screen: `THE IRON LAMP, STOLEN.` · `TOMORROW, A CLAY ONE.` · `FOR A LAMP, HE BECAME A THIEF.` · `THE CLAY LAMP SOLD FOR A FORTUNE.` · then, large: `A CLAY LAMP.`

segments.voice: Think of one small thing taken from you, recently or long ago: an object, some money, credit for your work, a seat, and notice how tightly you still hold it. Ask what your clay lamp would be here, the simple, cheap thing that gives the same light. Then rest on what you still have that no one could take.
Lychnos. Greek for the lamp Epictetus lost: an iron one, replaced for a little with a cheap clay lychnos, while the thief gave up his own honesty.
Your line: a clay lamp. The light was never in the iron. That's day four hundred two.

howItsDone: Many readers keep Epictetus' clay lamp as a shorthand for letting small losses go: replacing what's gone simply and refusing to give up their own calm or character over it.

chat.meaning: A person only loses what they have. For a lamp, the thief became a thief. And we rage at thieves because we admire what they take.

notes: Discourses 1.18 paraphrased: the iron lamp by the household gods, the noise at the window, 'tomorrow you'll find an earthen one', 'a man loses only what he has', and 'don't admire your clothes and you won't be angry with the thief'. Confirm.
'For a lamp he became a thief' is attributed in the script to 'elsewhere in the Discourses' (I believe 1.29); confirm the chapter.
Lucian, Adversus Indoctum 13: Epictetus' earthenware lamp bought for 3,000 drachmas. Confirm section number and amount.
The 'clay lamp' carry reads as 'a clay lamp'; title word 'The clay lamp' kept exactly.

Reviewer edit: the text does not say the theft happened at night; 'noise in the night' and 'empty shelf' changed to 'noise at the window' and 'empty spot by the shrine'. Lucian wrote some decades after Epictetus died (c. 135); 'a generation later' is approximate.
